$comment: Evidence-driven development: every claim Proofkin makes, and the evidence that proves it. Test ids are <target>::<path> as printed by cargo test with '::tests' removed (target: lib, bin, or an integration test file name). Live checks are names printed by scripts/live_test.py; a trailing * matches a prefix. Run: python scripts/evidence.py [--live]. See README 'Evidence-driven development'.

claims.claim: Agents authenticate each other by public key and refuse every key that is not on the allowlist, including peers learned through gossip.
live: worker1 refused intruder
intruder has no peers

claims.claim: Agents on different networks find and connect to each other over the internet using only their endpoint ids (no IPs, ports or --peer).
live: worker1 online with a ticket
worker2 found worker1 by id over the internet
boss connected to worker1
boss connected to worker2

claims.claim: Allowlisted peers discover each other by gossip and chat is delivered to every connected peer.
live: worker1 got chat
worker2 got chat

claims.claim: Two peers dialing each other at once end up with one connection and no join/leave flapping.
Peers see disconnects; a task in flight fails cleanly when its peer leaves, and departed peers can't be delegated to.
live: boss saw worker2 disconnect
worker1 saw worker2 disconnect
delegating to departed peer refused

claims.claim: Peer tasks run only in folders the owner shared with that peer, by default the profile's own data folder (.proofkin-data) (read-only). The agent's working folder and every other folder stay private, and folders are advertised to peers by name only, never by path.
live: boss's task ran in worker1's data folder
worker1 refused a folder it did not share with boss

claims.claim: A peer's task gets the lower of the peer's grant and the shared folder's maximum access, so a coding folder can be shared writable with one peer while the data folder stays read-only.
live: worker2 wrote p2p_live.txt in its workspace
worker2 audited boss's task with its grant

claims.claim: A task in flight survives its connection being replaced (e.g. both peers dialed each other at once): it keeps running and its result arrives over the connection that is kept. Requests sent while connections converge are re-sent on the kept connection and run exactly once.
live: digital worker ran boss's task on its owner's account

claims.claim: A peer can delegate tasks only if allowlisted with --delegate, and only within its hourly limit.
live: delegation without permission refused

claims.claim: Delegated tasks run on a peer that serves the provider and the result comes back; providers a peer doesn't serve are refused.
live: boss sees worker1 serving Copilot
boss sees worker2 serving Copilot
worker1 started task
worker2 started task
worker1 result back at boss
worker2 result back at boss
worker1 answer mentions task_request
worker2 wrote p2p_live.txt in its workspace
no task failures at boss

claims.claim: A peer's task gets the lower of the peer's own grant (default read-only) and the shared folder's maximum; peers can't raise it.
live: worker2 audited boss's task with its grant

claims.claim: Each agent uses only its own profile's identity, accounts and private provider instances, never the machine's global sign-in.
live: worker1 signed in as *
worker2 signed in as *
unsigned profile refused
4 distinct endpoint ids
allowlists written
worker1 uses its own account
worker2 uses its own account
worker1's Copilot instance used its own COPILOT_HOME
worker2's Copilot instance used its own COPILOT_HOME

claims.claim: Tasks can't read files outside the workspace or credential files inside it (Copilot and Claude), and secrets never reach the requesting peer.
live: outside read result back at boss
secret never reached boss

claims.claim: Writes need workspace-write access, stay in the workspace, and can't plant files that run code later (.git hooks, editor tasks, agent settings).
Only the tools of the granted access level are offered; web, memory and sub-agents are never available to tasks, and MCP tools only from servers the folder's owner offers (MCP-1, MCP-2).

Shell commands need full access and run in an OS sandbox with no network and no bypass; obvious escapes are refused before they run. The sandbox confines the model's commands only: the MCP servers a task may use (its folder owner's, and the checks server) run with the owner's rights, as at the other access levels and as the checks after the model.
The web UI is reachable only from this machine with the per-run token (DNS rebinding refused), sets a strict CSP, and runs tasks.

Any agent, including a boss that only delegates, can allowlist peers from the web UI; folder grants are checked only for peers that may delegate. A refused connection shows in the activity feed with the peer's endpoint id, so the page offers to allowlist it (a teammate who allowlisted this agent first), and a new agent with nobody on its allowlist shows its first steps there.
Every task a peer asks an agent to run is recorded in the profile's audit log (peer, provider, access, outcome, duration) without the prompt text.
live: worker1 audited boss's tasks
worker2 audited boss's task with its grant
worker2 audited the refused request from worker1
audit logs hold no prompt text

claims.claim: When a task can edit files, its result lists the workspace files it added, modified or deleted (build output and .git ignored).
live: boss sees the files worker2's task changed

claims.claim: A requester can cancel a delegated task: the worker stops the provider run, frees the task slot and audits it as cancelled. Tasks of a requester that disconnects are cancelled too.
live: boss cancelled a running Copilot task on worker1
worker1 audited the task as cancelled

claims.claim: Running tasks can be cancelled from the web UI and show as cancelled.
The agent's owner sees the audit log in the web UI (token-protected, no prompt text).

An owner can create digital workers: each is its own peer (key, allowlist, shared folders, audit log) but has no accounts of its own. It runs tasks signed in as its owner, can't be signed in separately, and digital workers can't own other workers.
live: digital worker ran boss's task on its owner's account

claims.claim: Peers see a digital worker's owner and role, and the role guides every task the worker runs.
live: boss sees the digital worker's owner and role

claims.claim: From its web UI (or the command line) an owner creates digital workers that run on its sign-ins (it can sign in to Copilot there with a GitHub CLI account, refused unless it works) in folders it picks, which a worker shares as its owner does. The owner's agent runs each as a background agent that dials it, starts the ones that start with it whenever it starts, and stops them cleanly when it stops. The owner starts, stops and deletes them there: deleting stops a worker, takes it off the owner's allowlist and out of its squads (a squad left empty goes) and deletes its profile, keeping its data folder; one running outside the owner's agent isn't deleted until it stops, one that stops on its own shows why, and a profile runs in one agent at a time.
live: worker1's agent started its digital worker helper
digital worker ran boss's task on its owner's account
stopping worker1 stopped its digital worker, which was then deleted and left worker1's allowlist

claims.claim: A boss groups peers into squads; a squad step runs on an online member that serves the provider and the folder, preferring the least busy one.

Plans run steps in dependency order and in parallel where possible, give each step the tasks and results of the steps it depends on (each task cut at 1,000 characters, each result at 8,000, inside the same external-content envelope), skip steps whose prerequisites failed, and reject cycles and unknown steps before running anything.
live: boss's plan ran a dependent step with its prerequisite's result

claims.claim: The boss runs plans and sees squads (members, online, running tasks) in the web UI; a step's card keeps its folder (worker:docs) while it runs.

A task can ask the worker's runtime (not the model) to run the folder owner's checks after the model; the result carries their exit codes and output, failures are retried with the failure output, timed-out or cancelled checks are killed with everything they started, and only peers with full access may request them (peers see check names, never commands).
live: worker's runtime ran the owner's check after the model

claims.claim: Every delegated result carries evidence signed with the worker's identity key and bound to the exact output; the requester trusts it only if it is signed by the peer it sent the task to, and any change to the record or output is detected.
live: boss verified the worker's signature on the evidence

claims.claim: In a folder shared with --worktrees, each editing task works on its own git branch with hooks disabled; its work is committed and returned as a patch whose hash is signed (new files of build and tool caches the model made, such as __pycache__/, *.pyc, node_modules/ or a top-level target/, stay out unless the base commit has that folder, and the task's report names the files committed, the first 20 then how many more, and lists what was left out), the shared folder itself stays untouched, and another peer can apply the patch in its own worktree to check the work independently; a patch can't create symlinks or files the model itself may not write.
live: worker committed the task on its own branch and returned the patch

claims.claim: Plans declare claims; a claim is proven only by finished steps backed by verified runtime evidence (passing checks or a sign-off), never by a model's word, failed checks or a bad signature. Every plan run is saved with a report, and re-verifying it from run.json alone checks each signature, that each record was requested by the run's boss, signed by the step's peer, produced during the run and not reused, and recomputes the verdict from that.
live: boss's evidence run proved its claims
the saved run's signatures re-verify offline

claims.claim: A plan step can ask a team member (or the boss's own user) to approve: the request shows the work it is about, the answer is signed with the approver's key, a rejection fails its claim, and cancelling the plan withdraws the request.
live: teammate's signed approval came back

claims.claim: The web UI marks results that carry valid signed evidence, lists evidence runs with their report and a fresh signature check, and lets the user answer approval requests (a rejection needs a reason).

Plan steps save their verified results into the profile's private knowledge base (save=) and later steps get that knowledge in their prompt (context=); unverified results never become knowledge, topics are plain names, and a plan naming a missing topic is refused before anything runs.
live: boss saved the verified result as knowledge

claims.claim: Ready-made playbooks cover the lifecycle: bootstrap a fresh project, reverse-engineer an existing one into knowledge, take a change through design, independent verification, security, privacy and compliance gates, and learn from operations. Each renders into a valid plan where every claim is proven only by runtime checks or a sign-off, and explains itself before use (each step in plain words, what it proves, what you need).

Monitors run a folder owner's check on a schedule; every run is a metric sample, and the ops report shows availability against each SLO, latency, incidents and how they ended, peer task and evidence run statistics.
live: monitors recorded metrics and the ops report shows them

claims.claim: Repeated monitor failures open an incident and alert the team (a teammate who isn't connected gets the alerts it missed when it connects); a matching troubleshooting guide's fix runs first, otherwise the debugging agent diagnoses read-only. A fix it names with high confidence runs and, if the monitor then passes, becomes a new active TSG; unsure or failed fixes leave a draft TSG and escalate to a person.
live: a troubleshooting guide fixed the incident without the model
the debugging agent diagnosed an incident no guide covers
the team was alerted by chat

claims.claim: The web UI shows health (monitors against SLOs, open incidents counted once per monitor however often they were opened, monitors that can't run with how to fix them, the incident log, the last 24 hours' task statistics and evidence runs), the knowledge base with its TSGs, and fills in playbooks into the plan editor.

An open incident stays open across agent restarts: the same failure never opens a second incident, alert or debugging run, and all of a monitor's open incidents resolve when it passes again. A monitor whose folder or check is gone shows it can't run, with the fix, and records no samples, incidents or model calls; monitors follow the agent's current shares without a restart.

Monitors are managed in the web UI's Health panel: it says what each monitor checks and how often, offers the folders' checks a new one can run, adds monitors (an unknown check or a taken name is refused) and removes them, closing their open incidents. A running agent follows monitors added, changed or removed, in the web UI or the CLI, within seconds and without a restart.

The web UI's task list outlives a restart: the latest 200 tasks are kept in the profile with long outputs cut, a task the agent stopped in the middle comes back cancelled saying why (reported once), unless it is a step of a plan run that goes on (PLAN-2), task ids go on from the kept ones, and Clear finished lets the finished tasks go while running ones stay.

The web UI shows a task's prompt and a team step's text as Markdown (code spans, bold, lists, rules, code blocks and paragraphs; a line of ---, *** or ___ after a blank line is a rule, so a signed result's summary shows under one; a code block ends only at a fence at least as long as its own, so one in a longer fence stays inside it; built as DOM nodes so markup in the text stays text), compactly; a long prompt is cut at about four lines with a fade until Show all.

A plan step's task text continues on the lines indented under it, keeping lists, paragraphs and deeper indentation, with options only on the step line and errors naming the step's first line; the plan editor and builder read and write those lines with their step.

A web UI plan run goes on after its agent restarts, as the same run: it is kept in the profile (runs-in-progress) as its steps are sent and end, and when the agent starts again (once its peers are connected, or after 30 seconds) its steps that ended keep their results and patches and aren't run or reported again, a step that was running is waited for again under the same request (its peer goes on with it, or sends the result it kept if it finished meanwhile, so it doesn't run twice), a sign-off is asked again under the same request, and the steps after them run; its issues on GitHub are the ones it had (nothing is made, linked or put on the board again), and it is saved once, when it ends. Its steps aren't cancelled when the agent stops (their peers keep them for the task grace), its tasks come back running rather than cancelled, and a cancelled or ended run isn't kept. Task ids go on after a restart (next-task-id), so a peer never takes a new task for one it is still running.

A plan can end with a pull request step (name after steps pr @peer:folder [title]): the folder's agent opens the pull request from the branch of the work before it in that folder (the step whose branch has the others' work through apply=; separate branches, a step without a folder, a squad, @me and model options are refused by the plan check), titled with the step's words or else those of the step that started the work. It is sent only to a folder whose owner lets peers open pull requests there (share pull-requests, or Takes pull request steps in the web UI; only folders with worktrees, and older agents never say so) and to a peer with edit access; the folder's agent opens it only for work it signed for that peer, with the branch's head still the step's commit, and runs no model. The step waits, saying the pull request is open with its link, until it is merged (done, with a signed record) or closed without being merged (failed); a second try finds the pull request it opened.

The system keeps learning: the ops summary (health, incidents, usage) is written into the knowledge base (kb learn, and hourly by agents with monitors) for context=all and the learn playbook, and learned TSGs fix repeats without the model.
live: kb learn wrote the ops summary into the knowledge base

claims.claim: Plan steps follow named skills (skill=): built-in instructions cover every playbook step (bootstrap, reverse engineering, design, implementation, review, security, privacy, compliance, ops insights, TSG writing) and the debugging agent follows incident-debugging; a profile's own skills add to or replace them, and unknown skills are refused before anything runs.

Before a plan runs it is checked against what exists now: connected peers, the folders they share with you with their checks, access and worktrees, squads, knowledge topics and skills. A plan with errors is refused with every reason, in the terminal and the web UI, and the web UI checks plans as you type. A malformed line is explained with what a step line looks like, repeating a list option adds to it (one-value options can't be repeated), and options typed into the task text are flagged (text in backticks isn't). A claim that would end unverified (nothing proves it, or a step without checks claims it) is flagged on the step, saying why, with the changes that fix it: let a sign-off prove it, add your sign-off, use the folder's own check, or remove the claim.
live: a plan with errors was refused before anything ran

claims.claim: A profile signs in to GitHub with a GitHub CLI account. Linking a repository clones it with that account (the token never reaches a command line or the clone's config) into a folder outside the profiles, shared with a worktree per task; the clone syncs, task branches are listed and pushed (only p2p/... ones), and pull requests open with the profile's account. Linking needs a sign-in.
live: linked a GitHub repository with the profile's GitHub sign-in

claims.claim: A profile's GitHub account gets a scope it lacks without a terminal: Grant access (on the Tracker card when the board lacks the project scope, which the tracker names, or on the GitHub card) and proofkin github grant run the GitHub CLI's device flow and show its one-time code and where to enter it. gh's active account is switched to the profile's for the refresh only if needed, and switched back afterwards, also when the flow fails, is cancelled, times out or the agent stops; afterwards the token is checked for the scopes. One flow runs at a time, scope names are checked, an account the GitHub CLI doesn't have is refused, and a profile not signed in to GitHub (or a digital worker) can't grant.

Another GitHub account signs in from the web UI (Sign in another account, with the project and workflow scopes ticked) or with proofkin github login --new: the GitHub CLI's device flow shows its code in a dialog, the profile then uses the new account, and gh's previously active account is made active again. A new sign-in's host and scopes are checked before gh starts. The GitHub card shows what each scope of the profile's token is for, and gh's active account when it is another one.

Built-in checks validate a feature's spec package before any code: spec:spec (user stories with testable Given/When/Then or 'must' acceptance criteria tied to stories, security and privacy covered), spec:api (an OpenAPI 3 REST contract whose operations name their criteria and whose examples match their schemas, with success and client-error responses), spec:ux (a self-contained prototype showing every story, no external resources or server calls) and spec:trace (every criterion covered by the API or the prototype and claimed in evidence/claims.json). spec init writes a starter package that passes them all.
live: spec init scaffolds a spec package that passes every spec check

claims.claim: Peers run the built-in spec checks in the runtime, after the model, with any access level (they only read files, in-process, never following symbolic links), and sign the results as evidence; the folder's own checks still need full access, and plan checks know the difference.
live: worker2 proved the spec package with the built-in checks, without full access

claims.claim: The spec playbook takes a feature from spec to REST API contract to UX prototype to claims, each step following a skill (write-spec, api-contract, prototype-ux, spec-to-claims), building on the previous step's commit and proven by built-in checks, then accepted by the product owner and the tech lead; implement-spec builds it with a test per acceptance criterion, verified independently.
live: boss's spec-driven run proved its claims

claims.claim: UX prototypes and review packs are previewed from the web UI at an unguessable, expiring capability URL, in a CSP sandbox (opaque origin, no network, no form posts), behind the Host check; only the prototype files and design and review documents a step's patch created (or a shared folder holds, without following links) are served, within size limits.

An approval step sends the approver (this agent's user or a teammate) what the steps before it created, directly or through other approvals: the UX prototype, or the review pack of decks, design documents and prototype, so they look before they answer.
live: the approver got the prototype a worker2 step created

claims.claim: Built-in checks prove a feature's SDLC design package, traced to its spec: design:arch (context, component, UML class or ER and sequence/state diagrams in valid Mermaid; a workflow per user story; ADRs with status, context, decision, alternatives and consequences, all listed in the architecture), design:data (a data dictionary covering every API schema property with classification, and purpose and retention for personal data; a data flow diagram with trust boundaries and protected boundary flows carrying all personal data), design:threats (STRIDE threats with mitigations, all six categories, every boundary flow covered, no open high risk), design:tests (a test for every acceptance criterion and high-risk threat, API-served criteria tested at contract, integration or e2e level) and design:ops (rollout, rollback, an SLO with a target, metrics, dashboard, alerts with actions, runbooks). design init writes a starter that passes them all.
live: design init scaffolds a design package and review pack that pass every check

claims.claim: The design playbook takes an accepted spec through architecture and ADRs, data, threats, test and operations plans and a review pack, each step following its skills (architecture-design, adr, data-design, threat-modeling, test-strategy, operability-design, review-*) and proven by built-in checks that need only read access; then the tech lead, the security and privacy champions and the product owner review it, and leadership last.
live: worker2 proved the design package and review pack with the built-in checks

claims.claim: review:decks holds each review document to its audience's form: Marp decks for the technical review (at most 30 slides; architecture, ADRs, API, data, threats, tests, operations, open questions; cites existing ADR and threat ids), the product review (at most 20; problem, every user story, prototype, scope, success metrics, release plan, decisions) and the leadership review (at most 12; summary first, impact, timeline, risks, ask; under 91 words a slide, no code or internal ids), and a customer feedback document (what we heard, what we're building, benefits, what's not included, at least 3 questions, next steps; no internal ids, security details or email addresses).

Review decks render as self-contained slide shows (speaker notes from comments, keyboard navigation, all-slides view, print to PDF, light and dark) and design documents as pages, from the CLI (design render) and in previews; raw HTML is shown as text and links can't run script.
live: design render wrote the review pack as HTML slide shows and pages

claims.claim: Content from outside a task (earlier steps' results, knowledge topics, check output, incident text, MCP tool results) reaches the model inside an external-content envelope it can't close or reopen, with a standing rule to treat it as data, never as instructions (prompt-injection spotlighting); people see approval requests without the rule.
live: boss's plan ran a dependent step with its prerequisite's result
the MCP tool result reached the model inside the external-content envelope

claims.claim: Results, failing check output and the check commands, error messages, knowledge topics and incident alerts leave the machine with known secret formats redacted (private keys and PGP key blocks, GitHub, AWS access and secret keys, Slack, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and npm tokens, JWTs, connection strings, signed URLs, bearer tokens, password settings such as DB_PASSWORD=), with a note of how many; check output is redacted before it is cut to its end, so a key printed early can't leak in part, and the evidence is signed for the redacted output.

A shared folder's owner offers MCP servers to peers' tasks (a local command or an https URL, the tools tasks may call, the least access needed); peers learn only the names they may use and what their owner says each is for, never commands, variables, headers or URLs, and the owner's web UI shows them without their secrets. A task gets only the servers it asks for (mcp= in a plan step, or picked in the web UI) that its folder offers at its access; Codex tasks can't use them, and plans are checked before they run.
live: a Copilot task on worker2 used the MCP server its owner offered

claims.claim: A task's model can call only the allowed tools of its own MCP servers: Copilot gets them in its tool allowlist (under names no built-in tool can have) and its permission handler approves only those servers and tools; Claude gets them as pre-approved tools and its tool hook refuses any other.
live: the MCP server ran only the tool its owner allowed

claims.claim: Plans and playbooks run on their own at set times (every N minutes, hours or days, daily, on weekdays or given days, in local time) while the agent runs: due schedules start without overlapping themselves, a run missed while the agent was off runs once when it starts (when its peers are back), and each run is a saved evidence run whose verdict is recorded; schedules are managed from the CLI and the web UI (add, pause, resume, run now, delete).
live: boss ran a missed scheduled plan on its own as an evidence run

claims.claim: The rehearse playbook rehearses a feature's reviews before they happen: agents on a squad play the tech lead, the security and privacy champions, the product owner, leadership and a customer in parallel (stakeholder-simulation skill), and a synthesis (feedback-synthesis skill) writes the rehearsal, proven by review:rehearsal (readiness, each audience's likely verdict, a severity and an action for every concern, at least 3 prepared answers), before the owner decides what to fix. spec check runs review:rehearsal once a rehearsal exists.
live: design init scaffolds a design package and review pack that pass every check

claims.claim: A profile imports plugins from a folder, a GitHub repository (private ones with the profile's GitHub sign-in) or a git URL, in the layouts GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code and Agent Plugins use, or picks one from a marketplace; its owner reviews what a plugin contains (skills, agents, MCP servers and the values they need, what isn't used) before anything is kept, and importing runs nothing: commands, hooks and LSP servers are listed and left out.
live: a plugin was imported with its skill, agent and MCP server, and nothing in it ran

claims.claim: A plugin's skills guide plan steps like the profile's own (by name when no other skill has it, always as plugin.skill), and its MCP servers are templates its owner offers in a folder with the values they need, the access and the tools; turning a plugin off withdraws both, updating it pauses offered servers that would now start differently, and removing it removes the servers it offered.
live: a plugin's skill guided a plan step
a plugin's MCP server, offered while worker2 ran, served boss's task

claims.claim: A plan step can act as an agent (agent=NAME): a role with instructions, the skills it follows and the MCP servers it uses. Agents are Markdown files with front matter (lists in any YAML form) that an owner adds in the web UI or the CLI, or that a plugin brings; a plugin's agent follows the plugin's own skills, and the tools and model fields of an agent file are left out with a note. The step gets the agent's instructions before its skills, and the agent's skills and MCP servers along with its own; an unknown agent, a sign-off acting as an agent, or an agent whose MCP servers the step's folder doesn't offer is refused before anything runs. A profile's agent names only skills that exist; a plugin's agents are withdrawn when it is turned off and can't be removed apart from it.
live: a plugin's agent brought its instructions, skill and MCP server to a plan step

claims.claim: Owners configure MCP servers in the web UI and the CLI: offer one by hand, from an MCP configuration (mcp.json, .mcp.json or VS Code's, placeholders filled in for the folder) or from a plugin, with secret values typed hidden and never shown again; pause, resume, change or remove it. Changes reach a running agent's peers within seconds, also when made from the CLI, and concurrent changes never overwrite each other (a lock file its last holder is still deleting is waited for, on Windows too).
live: the plugin's secret value isn't shown
pausing a server from the CLI withdrew it from the running agent's peers

claims.claim: Owners add their own skills in the web UI (pasted or loaded from a file, named by its front matter) or the CLI (skill import of a SKILL.md, its folder or a Markdown file, at most 64 KB), and remove them; built-in skills can be replaced but not removed, and a plugin's go with their plugin.

MCP tool results reach the model inside the external-content envelope: Copilot sessions rewrite each MCP tool's result in a post-tool hook, keeping its shape, and run no repository hooks; Claude's post-tool hook does the same; prompts of tasks that use MCP servers carry the standing rule. Server names stay unambiguous, so a task can't reach another server's tools.
live: the MCP tool result reached the model inside the external-content envelope

claims.claim: A due scheduled run that can't start (e.g. its peer is still reconnecting after a restart) is tried again every two minutes for an hour, then recorded as missed with why; Run now says why it can't start; resuming counts from now without a made-up run; a run that crashes never leaves its schedule stuck as running; schedules are edited in the web UI with a picker that previews the next runs.

The web UI follows written UX guidelines (docs/ux-guidelines.md): the plan box and its main button stay usable at every window size (below 1180 px the conversation keeps the window's height and stays in view while the page scrolls), with a full-size plan editor whose palette adds peers, folders, squads, checks, MCP servers, skills, agents and knowledge to the step at the cursor in the place the plan syntax expects (repeated skills add up) or starts a new step with them, never pasting raw text; the plan check's fixes are buttons that change the plan; a plan builder edits the same plan as forms (claims, then a card per task or sign-off) that can't express the usual mistakes: tasks prove claims only with a check, no step can wait for one that waits for it, renames and removals carry through, what a field still needs is said on it, and Run goes to the first; playbooks are picked from cards that say what each does, proves and needs, not from a dropdown; every dialog closes with Escape; destructive actions ask in the page; secrets never reach the page; the theme color follows the theme; times show their day unless it is today, and counts agree; a new agent shows its first steps (share the ticket, add a teammate's, or create a digital worker).
The Claude/Codex bridge passes task fields, runs requests concurrently, and surfaces provider errors and bridge exits.

A Copilot CLI that updated itself past the protocol this build's Copilot SDK speaks doesn't take Copilot down: agents use the newest earlier version the CLI keeps in its package cache that speaks it, and say so; with none (or when COPILOT_CLI_PATH names the CLI), the error says which protocols differ and how to fix it, and doctor checks the protocol rather than trusting the version.
The command line definition is valid (no conflicting flags or subcommands).

Installs from before the rename to Proofkin keep working: settings under their old names (P2PAGENTS_HOME, P2PAGENTS_SECRET_STORE, ...) apply when the PROOFKIN_* ones are unset, profiles stay in ~/.p2pagents while there is no ~/.proofkin, and data, repository and worktree folders that exist keep their old names (new ones get the new names).

Spec Kit features and OpenSpec changes become evidence plans: a claim per user story (its acceptance scenarios), functional requirement or added and modified requirement, proven by the folder's tests in an implementation step and again on a reviewer's copy, and success criteria proven by a sign-off; removed and renamed requirements and edge cases become instructions; the spec, cut to fit a prompt, is saved as a knowledge topic the steps are given; a folder with several specs lists them to pick from; open questions and missing parts are flagged; spec files must be regular files inside the spec's folder, at most 1 MB (links out of it, devices and pipes are refused unread), and spec text can't add plan lines. It works from the command line, the web UI's implement-speckit playbook and the import_spec MCP tool.

Other agents connect over MCP (Streamable HTTP: the stateless 2026-07-28 revision, whose headers must match the body, with server/discover; and the initialize-based revisions before it) with the profile's integration token: off until the owner turns it on, valid only for MCP and A2A (and the web UI's token not there), refused from other sites' pages, and dead as soon as it's turned off. Their       tools list peers, delegate tasks to peers (never this machine), check and run plans and return their evidence reports, and their work shows up as the owner's tasks; a delegate, run_plan or get_task call that waits and comes with a progress token and Accept: text/event-stream is answered as a stream of notifications/progress (the work's status each time it changes, with an increasing progress) and then its result, on both revisions, while any other request gets one JSON body; what they send is size-capped, and only the latest finished tasks are kept (the oldest go first, a plan's steps together).

claims.claim: Other agents connect over A2A 1.0: an agent card (only while connecting is on) with the JSON-RPC interface and the bearer scheme; SendMessage runs a task on a peer or a plan, waiting for the result unless returnImmediately is set, with the peer's output, each step's output and the evidence verdict as artifacts; GetTask, ListTasks (by context, artifacts on request) and CancelTask; SendStreamingMessage and SubscribeToTask stream a task live as server-sent events (the task, a status update with the progress each time it changes, and the finished task last; a finished task can't be subscribed to); other versions, files, an extended card, finished and unknown tasks get A2A's errors, and work that can't start comes back as a rejected task (an error when streaming).

claims.claim: A task run on its own (outside a plan) proves its work like a plan step: the web UI's Run task asks for the folder's checks (offered only where the user has full access, with attempts while they fail), and a task that asked for checks or got a commit back is kept as a one-step evidence run that claims its checks pass (T-1), titled with what it was about; its card, and every plan step's, links to its run. Checks are refused for this agent's own tasks, which no peer's runtime checks.

Anyone can verify a run without trusting the agent that ran it: the web UI downloads its run.json exactly as saved (nothing outside the runs folder), proofkin runs verify --file re-checks one from anywhere under any name (signatures and outputs; patches need the run folder), and verification names who requested the run and only the keys that signed its evidence.

claims.claim: Pull requests carry their proof: the runtime that commits a task's work keeps the evidence record it signed as a git note on the commit (refs/notes/proofkin), and opening a pull request from the branch (repo pr, or the web UI, on by default) checks the record's signature and that it covers the branch's head, then adds who made the commit, for whom (by the name this agent's allowlist has for the requester) and what the task was part of (from its audit log), its key and the checks run on the change with their results (never their commands), plus the verdict and claims of this profile's evidence run that holds the record. Opening the pull request also pushes the notes ref to the repository (best effort: if that fails the pull request still opens and the proof says the record stays on this machine), and the proof says how to fetch it. A missing, moved or forged record adds nothing, and the text is redacted before it leaves the machine.

claims.claim: A peer working on a task says what it is doing as it changes: its place in the queue for a task slot, each model attempt (told what failed before it), each check its runtime runs, and committing the work. The requester sees it live (CLI, web UI, and MCP and A2A task status), and each serving agent tells its peers how busy it is (tasks running and queued, and how many of them are theirs). A task says what it is part of on the requester's side (a step of a run, or a task), which the worker's activity and audit log show. Older peers ignore the new messages and fields.
live: boss saw live what worker1 was doing on its step

claims.claim: A dropped connection doesn't fail tasks at once: they say they are reconnecting, and carry on if the peer comes back within the task grace (60 s by default), their results arriving over the new connection. An agent that stops on purpose tells its peers first: the tasks it runs for them fail at once, saying it stopped, and the tasks it gave them are cancelled.

A squad step goes to the member least busy with everyone's tasks (as members report them, plus the boss's own tasks waiting on them, counted as they are sent). A step a member turns down (e.g. over the hourly limit) or loses moves to another member, saying why. A step that takes longer than its timeout= is cancelled on its peer and fails with the reason, and the steps that depend on it are skipped.

A plan step can hand its work to a lead's team (team @lead:folder): the lead runs its owner's team plan for that folder, with the task filled in, on its own peers under its own allowlist, reports each team step upward as it goes, and signs its result with the whole team run inside, which its audit log records as a team step. A claim on the boss's step is proven only if that team run passed and every signature in it checks out, all the way down (a team run changed after signing doesn't). Team steps need edit access in a folder that takes them, go no more levels down than levels= allows (at most 3), and never hand work back to an agent it came from.
live: a team step went through worker2's team to worker1's real Copilot, signed all the way down
worker2 led the team run for boss's team step

claims.claim: The web UI shows a plan as one card (a bar of its steps' states, the steps in the order they can run, Cancel plan and its evidence run), with what each running step's peer is doing now. A team step is labelled as one and shows its lead's team steps live, then the team run it came back with; the lead's page shows the team run as a plan of its own, for the peer whose step it is. The plan editor checks team steps as they are written (team, levels=, timeout=, and the options a team step can't take).

A folder's owner can leave its team plans to their agent's model instead of writing one (proofkin share team NAME --model, optionally --approve; a written plan and the model exclude each other, and peers see either as a folder that takes team steps). For each team step it is handed, the lead's model writes the team plan with the owner's default model and effort for its first provider, read-only in the folder, holding a task slot only while it writes, from a prompt with the task as handed down, how a team plan is written and the team it may use (its peers except the agents the work came from, its squads and skills).       The plan is the answer's first fenced block, checked as an owner's plan is before it runs; one that doesn't check out goes back to the model with what is wrong, up to 3 tries in all, and then fails the step. With --approve the owner approves each plan first: they may ask for changes, at most twice, which the model makes before they are asked again, and a plan they reject fails the step. The team run's plan (in a comment) and the lead's answer say whose model wrote it for whose step, and whether the owner approved it and after how many rounds of changes. A lead that runs no models refuses such team steps.

The web UI lets an owner have a folder's model write its team plans (Team plan…: who writes it, I do or My model writes one for each team step, with Ask me to approve each plan before it runs): PUT /api/shares/NAME/team with {"model": true, "approve": bool} saves it for the running agent and in shares.json, and the reply, the activity and the page's shares (team_model, team_approval) say what the folder does now. A written plan and the model replace each other, DELETE removes either, and a body that says neither or both is refused with what to send, as the data share and a folder it doesn't share are.

With a tracker linked (a repository and, optionally, a GitHub Project), each plan run is tracked on GitHub: the run gets an issue (or works on an existing one with track: #N; track: <title> names a new one and track: off leaves the run untracked) and each step a sub-issue of it (or an existing issue named with issue=#N, made a sub-issue of the run's), assigned to the profile's GitHub account and blocked by the issues of the steps it runs after. On the board each item says which agent does it (an Agent field, added if the board has none).       A later run on the same issue takes up its steps' open sub-issues again, unless a run at the same time works on them: then it makes its own. A plan can't give two steps one issue, or a step the run's own.

The board follows a tracked run: a step's item is In progress while it runs (with the peer doing it, moved once however often the peer reports), In review while its committed work waits for a pull request or its sign-off for a person, and Done once closed; a step that changed no files is closed when it is done; a failed or skipped step goes back to Todo. Each result and failure is commented on its issue with its signed evidence (signer, checks, commit and branch), and the run's issue gets the verdict and its claims; it is closed once all its sub-issues are, waiting in review while its own steps' pull requests are open (and where it was while other work is), and it goes back to where it was if the run failed. Without the project scope tracking keeps to the issues and says how to grant it, and tracking never fails or holds up the plan's steps.

A tracked step's task carries its issue and those of the steps whose work it applies. The worker's commit references them in Refs: trailers (only well-formed owner/repo#N references, since they come from a peer, as is the subject a step that works on an issue asks for, of which only the first line is used), its task branch lists them, and a pull request opened from the branch (repo pr or the web UI) closes them, so GitHub links the pull request to the issues and closes them when it merges.

A profile links its tracker with its GitHub account (proofkin tracker link, or the web UI's Tracker card), which checks the repository and the board (a project given by its address or owner/number) and shows the board's statuses, or why the board isn't used and the command that fixes it. Every request is GitHub GraphQL through the GitHub CLI, on stdin, with the token only in gh's environment.       The board's items (or the open issues) are listed by status with their agent, assignees, sub-issue progress and closing pull requests, and Plan it starts a plan on an item with a step per open sub-issue; tracker add (or Add existing issues) puts the repository's issues and pull requests on the board with a status from their state (open issues to do, open pull requests in review, closed and merged ones done), keeping statuses already set. Tracked steps, plans and runs link their issues, and the plan editor knows track: and issue=.

The Tracker card, tracker status and tracker sync say what each run issue left open is waiting for: the run's number, title and link, how many of its sub-issues are closed, and each open sub-issue with the pull request that will close it, or that no pull request does yet. They are read in one GraphQL query and returned as waiting by GET /api/tracker and POST /api/tracker/sync, which also returns the run issues it closed. Runs that are closed or gone are left out.

The Work IQ client speaks MCP over streamable HTTP to a configurable endpoint (default https://workiq.svc.cloud.microsoft/mcp). It sends initialize (protocol 2025-06-18, client info proofkin and its version) and then notifications/initialized, keeps the Mcp-Session-Id and sends it with the MCP-Protocol-Version on later requests, and starts a new session once, sending the request again, when a request with a session gets 404. Every request carries Accept, Content-Type, a bearer token from the TokenSource and a new client-request-id in UUID v4 form. JSON and Server-Sent Events replies are both read (the SSE response is the event answering the request, skipping notifications). tools/list is cached per client and a tool the server doesn't offer is a clear error. The request-id, x-ms-request-id, client-request-id and x-ms-correlation-id of a response are kept with the result and with errors. The messages go through a Transport trait so a stdio transport can reuse the client.

Work IQ errors are classified and only the safe ones are retried. A WorkIqError has a class (sign in again, consent, denied by policy, billing, throttled with its delay, transient, uncertain change, other tool error), the request and correlation ids and a fix saying what to do and who can do it, and its message is one line: what happened, the fix, the ids. The class comes from the HTTP status (401, 402, 403, 429, 5xx), a WWW-Authenticate invalid_token or insufficient_claims challenge, JSON-RPC errors, tool results with isError, and payloads with stoppedReason error, errorCode, recoveryAction and retryAfterSeconds (under application/vnd.ms-workiq.retrieval and at the top level); AADSTS65001 and consent_required mean consent, AADSTS50105 and AADSTS53003 a denial with the admin's fix, spending policy and billing errors billing. A 401 makes the TokenSource refresh once and the call is sent once more (a failed refresh is reported with its reason). A throttled read waits for Retry-After or retryAfterSeconds when it is at most 60 seconds, at most twice. A transient failure of a read tool (retrieve, ask, fetch, fetch_blob, search_paths, get_schema, list_agents, discover) is retried at most twice with exponential backoff and jitter. Policy denials, consent, billing and every other tool, including the change tools, are never sent again after a failure, and a change that timed out or lost its connection is reported as uncertain. Waiting goes through an injectable Sleeper so tests don't wait.

A profile can have a Work IQ account: ProfileConfig.workiq, left out of profile.json when absent, with the connection (hosted with tenant and client id, or the CLI with an optional tenant), the user (UPN, display name, tenant id) and when it was added. Nothing secret is in profile.json: the refresh token is in the profile's secret store under the key workiq. The token source for a hosted account keeps the access token and its expiry in memory only, and refreshes it at the tenant's Entra token endpoint (grant_type refresh_token, client_id, refresh_token and the WorkIQAgent.Ask offline_access openid profile scope) five minutes before it expires. A new refresh token from Entra is saved and used for the next refresh. Callers at the same moment wait for one refresh, which also holds for the client's 401 refresh. invalid_grant and interaction_required are the sign-in-again class with the fix proofkin auth login workiq --profile P. A digital worker uses its owner's Work IQ account only when the owner turned that on for it (workiq_from_owner, set by proofkin worker create --workiq, which needs the owner signed in to Work IQ); otherwise the error says how. proofkin auth status shows the account, and proofkin auth logout workiq removes the account and its token.

proofkin auth login workiq --tenant T --client-id C [--device-code] --profile P signs a profile in to Work IQ. The browser flow is the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256 over a random verifier, a random state): a loopback listener on 127.0.0.1 with the redirect http://localhost:<port>, the browser opened (through a hook) and the URL printed, the authorize request with response type code, response mode query and the WorkIQAgent.Ask offline_access openid profile scopes and no resource parameter, the state checked (a wrong state is refused and the code is not used), the code exchanged with the verifier, and a page saying the window can be closed. The device code flow with --device-code prints Entra's message and polls the token endpoint at the interval given through authorization_pending and slow_down, and ends on expired_token and authorization_declined. The account (user, name and tenant from the unverified id token) is saved with the refresh token in the secret store, and the sign-in is checked right away with tools/list against Work IQ; if that fails the profile is signed out again. AADSTS65001 and consent_required (with the admin consent URL for the client id and tenant), AADSTS50105, AADSTS700016, AADSTS90002 and AADSTS7000218 are explained in clear words, also when Entra reports them in the browser redirect.

proofkin auth login workiq --cli [--account EMAIL] [--cli-path PATH] --profile P connects a profile to Microsoft's Work IQ CLI, which signs in by itself with its own app and picks the tenant from its account (--tenant is refused with --cli: the CLI has no tenant option): the sign-in finds the CLI (--cli-path, which must exist, else workiq on the PATH, else in npm's global folder from npm prefix -g, which a Node version manager keeps off the PATH) and saves the account (connection kind cli with the account given and where the CLI is) with no token in the secret store; the user shown is the account given, else the one the CLI reports in its initialize reply (serverInfo.user, else serverInfo.upn), else its default account (defaultAccount in workiq config show), else Work IQ CLI, and auth status and the doctor say '<user> through the Work IQ CLI'; the sign-in is checked right away with tools/list through the CLI and signed out again if that fails. A StdioTransport (the client's Transport over a child process) starts the CLI the sign-in found while it is there, else workiq on the PATH, else npx -y @microsoft/workiq, running mcp with --account when the account has one; it writes newline-delimited JSON-RPC to the child's stdin and reads replies line by line from its stdout, skipping notifications and lines that are not JSON and matching responses by id. The MCP client runs initialize, tools/list and tools/call over it. A child that exited is started again once, and gets the initialize handshake again before the message; a change tool that may already have reached a child that crashed is not sent again (reported as uncertain), and a second crash is an error. The child is killed when the transport is dropped. The child gets the agent's environment minus the inherited credential variables the providers' processes lose (GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY and the rest of INHERITED_CREDENTIAL_VARS). A CLI account has no bearer: its token source gives nothing. workiq::connect(profile) builds the client for the profile's account, hosted or CLI, and client_for_profile uses it. When the CLI says its EULA is not accepted (its error mentions the EULA or accept-eula), the error says to run workiq accept-eula yourself and that Proofkin never accepts it for you.

proofkin workiq doctor [--json] --profile P (docs/work-iq.md section 10) runs five checks in order against the account the profile uses, through workiq::connect_at, and stops at the first that fails; its address for the discovery document, the MCP endpoint and Entra are configurable (workiq::Endpoints) so tests use fakes. (1) Discovery, hosted accounts only (skipped otherwise): a GET of the protected-resource metadata answers with resource and authorization_servers. (2) Sign-in: the profile has a Work IQ account and, when hosted, its refresh token. (3) Token, hosted only: a fresh access token whose claims, decoded only for this diagnosis, have an aud of api://workiq.svc.cloud.microsoft or fdcc1f02-fc51-4226-8753-f668596af7f7, the account's tid, and WorkIQAgent.Ask in scp. (4) tools/list works and offers retrieve. (5) One small retrieve (query Proofkin connection check), audited with the purpose doctor and counted against the budgets. Each failure says what is wrong, the fix and who makes it, from the client's error classes where they apply: the Work IQ service principal (az ad sp create --id fdcc1f02-fc51-4226-8753-f668596af7f7, a tenant admin), admin consent (the adminconsent URL of the account's client id and tenant), user assignment (an admin, Enterprise applications, Users and groups), billing and the spending policy (a billing admin, Microsoft 365 admin center), the Work IQ MCP policy (an admin, Microsoft 365 admin center, Agents, Tools, Work IQ MCP), or signing in again (the user). --json prints the profile, whether all passed, and each check's name, result (ok, failed or skipped), detail and fix (who and action). The command exits 1 when a check fails. proofkin doctor shows one Work IQ line per profile (signed in or not, and the connection) without network calls.

The Work IQ content policy (src/workiq/content.rs, docs/work-iq.md section 3) reads retrieve results from structuredContent under application/vnd.ms-workiq.retrieval, never from the MCP content array, and fails on isError, stoppedReason error or a missing structuredContent. Only results whose contentProtection is exactly allowed (after trimming) are kept; the rest, a missing value included, are withheld and counted as missing, blocked or other. A Local audience gets every label; a Peer gets only the labels in its allowlist (compared without case), and unlabeled allows results without a label; results withheld by label are counted too. Markdown, titles and links are redacted, a result's title and date come from its resourceMetadata facet (document, email, meeting, chat or web; dates from sentTime, startTime and the Graph date names), results are kept by relevance when Work IQ scores them, else in Work IQ's order, up to a character cap (16000 by default), and each result is wrapped in the external-content envelope, followed by a Sources list (also wrapped) and a line with the withheld counts, under the heading saying the context is cited and unverified. Real results (Work IQ CLI 1.0.1: Files and Emails with a label object, Meetings and Chats without one, People without contentProtection) are read as such: labeled ones keep their displayName, unlabeled ones count as unknown and go to no peer, and People are withheld. An ask answer is read from structuredContent (answer, text, markdown or response), as Work IQ gives it, else from the result's text content; its citations come only from structuredContent, and an answer whose citations have no label metadata, or that has none, is local only: a Peer gets nothing from it.

A peer's Microsoft 365 grant (docs/work-iq.md section 4) is the optional m365 field of its entry in peers.json, left out when absent, with labels (the label names it may receive; unlabeled allows content without a label) and tools (its tasks may use this agent's Work IQ gateway, read only). Absent means nothing is allowed. proofkin peers allow <peer> --m365 General,Public,unlabeled [--m365-tools] sets it (names trimmed and without duplicates), --m365 off removes it, and running peers allow again without --m365 keeps the current grant; peers list shows it, and the web UI's peer JSON includes it read-only. The audience for content sent to a peer is Local for the owner's own digital workers, a Peer audience with the grant's labels for a granted peer, and none (refuse) for any other peer.

Microsoft 365 content keeps its origin (docs/work-iq.md section 4) and plans don't send it to peers not allowed to receive it. A knowledge topic with front matter origin: workiq and labels: (comma-separated) is marked (parse_mark, with_mark and KnowledgeBase::marks in src/knowledge.rs); a mark can be written into a topic with or without troubleshooting-guide front matter, a guide stays a guide, and a topic can have both. A step (Step.m365, a field the workiq= option and @workiq steps will set too) is marked when a context= topic is marked, with the union of the labels (context=all included), when a step it runs after is marked because it gets that step's output, and the steps that save= from a marked step write the mark into the topic, so a later step that uses it is marked. The plan check (preflight, with the allowlist and the owner's digital workers as Recipients) gives an error for a marked step whose target (a peer, a squad member the squad may pick, or the person asked to approve) has no Microsoft 365 grant or whose grant lacks one of the labels, naming the step, the peer, the labels and the proofkin peers allow command that grants them; a granted peer (labels compared without case) and the owner's digital workers get none. When the plan runs, the same check is made against the allowlist as it is then before each task is sent, and the step fails with the same message if the grant changed.

Every Work IQ call through Client::call_tool_in (done, failed or refused) appends one JSON line to <profile>/workiq-audit.jsonl (append only, behind a lock, a write error only warns): time, tool, purpose (step with the run id and step, knowledge import, gateway, doctor or command), audience (local or the peer's name), the query's SHA-256 and length and never its text, outcome (ok, refused, or the error class), the results and withheld counts and the labels seen when the result has them, the request, x-ms-request, client-request and correlation ids, and the duration. Budgets in profile.json (workiq_budget: calls_per_day, default 200; calls_per_run, default 25) are checked before a call is sent: a call over a budget fails with an over-budget error that names the budget and the proofkin workiq budget command that raises it, is not sent, and is audited as refused (refused calls don't count). Usage today and per run is counted from the log, the day being the local date from an injectable clock, so a new day resets the daily count. proofkin workiq usage --profile P prints today's use against the budgets and proofkin workiq budget --per-day N --per-run N --profile P changes them (a limit left out is kept; zero is refused).

The workiq= step option (all, or a comma list of email, meetings, files, teams, people and connectors) is parsed, refused for unknown sources (naming the known ones) and on approve steps, and taught to the plan editor (option list and round trip). all uses the copilot strategy with no capabilities, a list with connectors uses copilot with those capabilities, any other list uses grounding. The plan check needs the plan profile's Work IQ account (naming proofkin auth login workiq) and a target that is the owner's digital worker or a peer with a Microsoft 365 grant (naming the grant command); the step is marked, a peer gets at most its grant's labels, and a later step after a workiq= step on the owner's own worker gets a warning, not an error. When the step is sent, after its peer is picked, the agent searches Work IQ with the step's own words through the audited client (a call context for the run and step, so budgets apply), builds the retrieval section for that peer's audience and puts it before Your task: in the guarded prompt; the kept results' labels are the step's actual labels, which the send-time check of a later step uses. A Work IQ error or a budget refusal fails the step with its one-line message. The run record keeps per step the sources, labels, kept and withheld counts and request ids. The web UI's plan check, the plans it starts and its Work IQ import, and the agent's /plan command, read the profile's settings when they run, so a Work IQ sign-in made while the agent runs (proofkin auth login workiq in another process) counts at once.

A step whose target is @workiq is run by the plan's own agent, never sent to a peer: it calls Work IQ's ask tool through the audited client with the step's own words plus the results of the steps it runs after (capped like other steps), and agent=<id> (letters, digits and - _ . : @, at most 200 characters) is sent as agentId. Its output is the answer and its cited sources for the local audience; the step is marked as Microsoft 365 content with its citations' labels, and a citation without label information adds the label unknown, which no peers allow --m365 grant can include, so no peer gets that output (a later step on a peer without a grant, or with a narrower one, is refused). The answer reaches later steps through after, and save= writes the mark and a source note saying it was a Work IQ answer. Plan errors say an answer is context and never proof for claims=, verify=, apply=, mcp=, skill=, attempts=, levels=, team and approve on a @workiq step. The plan check needs the profile's Work IQ account. The run shows it as done by workiq (or workiq:<agent id>), with no evidence and not verified. proofkin workiq agents lists the agents list_agents returns (name and id), from structuredContent or, as Work IQ gives them, from the JSON list in the text content. The plan editor knows the @workiq target.

proofkin kb import workiq <topic> --query <text> [--from SOURCES] [--replace] runs Work IQ's retrieve through the audited client for the profile (purpose knowledge-import, the query on one line, --from taking the sources of the workiq= option with the same strategy and capabilities and the same refusals, default all), builds the retrieval section for the local audience and saves it as the topic: marked as Microsoft 365 content with the labels of the kept results (unknown for a result without label information), with the front matter lines query: and retrieved: (the date) and the source note Work IQ retrieve. An existing topic is not overwritten without --replace (and Work IQ is not asked), and when no result was kept nothing is written and the error says how many results were withheld and why. The saved topic works with context=, and its mark goes through the plan check to the steps that use it. POST /api/kb/import/workiq (topic, query, from, replace) is token-guarded, does the same and answers with the topic and the kept and withheld counts and labels.

A workiq= step's signed evidence records the Work IQ context its task had by hash, never its content: the plan's agent sends the task with where the Microsoft 365 section is in its prompt and how many results it held with their labels, and the worker refuses a task whose section isn't a whole part of its prompt, else signs context [{source workiq, sha256 of exactly that part, results, labels}] (a team step's lead too), and its result's summary says Work context from Microsoft 365 (Work IQ) with the count, labels and the start of the hash. The run record keeps the section's SHA-256, and the saved run keeps the section itself next to its run.json (<step>.workiq.md), never in it, so a run.json shared to be verified holds no Microsoft 365 content; runs verify fails a step whose evidence doesn't record the hash the run kept for it, or, given the run's folder, whose kept section no longer has its hash. Records without context sign as before; claims never rest on Work IQ content.

The Work IQ commands work through the program itself, as a user runs them, against a fake Work IQ and Entra: auth login workiq --device-code signs in, workiq doctor passes its five checks, workiq agents lists the agents, kb import workiq saves what the content policy keeps (withheld counted), and an agent started with proofkin --name runs a plan's @workiq step itself and sends a workiq= step to a peer with only the results its Microsoft 365 grant allows; runs verify passes and the step's signed evidence records the context by the hash of the section the run kept; workiq usage counts every call; each run uses the refresh token the run before saved (Entra rotates them); after auth logout workiq the doctor fails. The same commands work through the Work IQ CLI given with --cli-path. The test-only settings PROOFKIN_TEST_WORKIQ_URL and PROOFKIN_TEST_ENTRA_URL that point the program at the fakes take only a root http(s) address on the loopback interface (localhost or a loopback IP); any other value is refused, never replaced by the real service, so no token goes elsewhere.

A live check against a real tenant's Work IQ, behind PROOFKIN_LIVE_WORKIQ=cli|hosted (scripts/live_workiq.py; python scripts/evidence.py --live runs it when that is set), only reads: a fresh profile signs in to Work IQ (through the Work IQ CLI, or with Proofkin's device code sign-in), its doctor passes every check with one retrieve, proofkin workiq agents reads the agents list Work IQ gives (only how many is shown), and its agent runs a plan whose workiq= step goes to the profile's own digital worker on real Copilot and whose @workiq step gets Microsoft 365 Copilot's answer. The run's signed evidence verifies, the step's evidence records the Work IQ context by its hash and nothing else, and every call in the profile's Work IQ audit file was a read tool. Step outputs stay out of its log and email addresses are masked. Without PROOFKIN_LIVE_WORKIQ the check is not run and fails nothing.

A folder can offer Work IQ to its owner's tasks as its MCP server workiq (proofkin mcp add <folder> workiq --workiq [--tool ...]; the name is workiq, it has no command or URL, only tools that read: retrieve, ask, fetch, search_paths, get_schema, list_agents, and any task access may use it). A task that asks for mcp=workiq gets, for that task only, http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp/workiq/<session> with a random bearer; the agent calls Work IQ itself through the profile's audited client, so the model's MCP config holds no token. The session lists only the allowed tools Work IQ offers, never one whose MCP annotations say it changes things (readOnlyHint false or destructiveHint true), refuses any other tool before it reaches Work IQ, puts every result through the content policy for the task's audience (a peer audience gets only retrieve and ask, within its labels), audits each call with purpose gateway, needs its bearer, refuses requests with an Origin header, and closes when the task ends. A digital worker's owner's tasks see what Work IQ allows (peers: WIQ-17). A plan marks a step with mcp=workiq, and the steps after it, with the label unknown, so nothing made from what its model read goes to a peer.

A peer's task gets Work IQ through the gateway (mcp=workiq) only when the agent's owner granted that peer --m365-tools: its session then offers only retrieve and ask, whose results carry labels, and the content policy gives it only results with the labels of its grant; every call is audited with the peer's name as its audience. Without the grant the task is refused before its model starts, and the refusal names the grant to add (proofkin peers allow <peer> --m365 <labels> --m365-tools). The grant is read again when the task starts. The requester's plan marks the step's output unknown (WIQ-16), so it goes no further to a peer.

Importing Microsoft's Work IQ plugin (the shape of microsoft/work-iq:plugins/workiq: .github/plugin/plugin.json, skills/, and a .mcp.json whose server is the hosted https://workiq.svc.cloud.microsoft/mcp with oauthClientId) keeps its skills and makes its MCP server a Work IQ template: its own connection and sign-in settings are dropped, the review notes that it is offered through this agent's own Work IQ sign-in and gateway with only its tools that read, and offering it in a folder gives the agent's workiq server (no URL, command or headers; it must be named workiq). The Work IQ CLI's server (npx @microsoft/workiq mcp, or workiq mcp) is recognized the same way; other servers are not.

The web UI has a token-guarded API for the profile's Work IQ account, which reads the profile as its files are now, so a sign-in made in another process counts. GET /api/workiq answers whether the account the agent uses is signed in, its line, how it connects (hosted or cli), its user, the CLI's account and path for a CLI account, the profile it belongs to (a digital worker may use its owner's) and whether that is this profile, why a digital worker its owner didn't let use theirs has none (not_used), the sign-in command, and today's calls against the per-day and per-run budgets (with each run's calls). POST /api/workiq/doctor answers the doctor's checks with their results, details and fixes, always as 200. POST /api/workiq/sign-in (account, cli_path) signs the profile in through Microsoft's Work IQ CLI as proofkin auth login workiq --cli does and answers who signed in and the line; DELETE /api/workiq signs out, and is refused when not signed in; each adds a line to the activity. PUT /api/workiq/budget (per_day, per_run) sets the budgets. Errors are 400s in the sign-in's or set_budget's own words. A digital worker that uses its owner's account sees it but is refused signing in, signing out and budgets: its owner does those. The page's Work IQ card, after the GitHub card, shows this from GET /api/workiq and acts through these endpoints; every element its script looks up is on the page, and its sign-in and budget dialogs close with Escape and Cancel like the others.

Every task result names the model that did the work, as its provider says: Copilot from the CLI's usage events of the session's own agent (else the model the task asked for), Claude from the Agent SDK's init message, Codex from the thread's model or the top-level model of the profile's own config.toml. A worker sends it with the result (a field older peers ignore) and names it in the signed output's evidence summary, so the record vouches for it and older requesters verify it as before; names are cleaned to the characters model names use before they are shown. The web UI's task and step cards (after the provider), the worker's audit log, run records and reports, the tracker's step comments and the CLI's printed results show it; without a model the result is as before.
