claims.claim: A profile's owner sets each provider's default model and the models tasks may ask for (proofkin models default <provider> <model>|none and models allow <provider> <list>|any), kept in profile.json and left out when unset. A default must be allowed; with a list and no default, tasks that name none run on the first in the list. models list prints the models Copilot offers the account and marks the default and the allowed ones. A task that names no model runs on the default, an agent's executor limits Copilot sessions to the list, and its hello tells peers the defaults and lists of the providers it serves (older peers' hellos read as saying nothing), cleaned of malformed names. An agent definition's model: is kept (inherit and names that aren't model names are left out).

A task chooses its model: a plan step's model= option (given once, a model's name, not on sign-offs, team steps or @workiq steps; a step with agent= and no model= takes the agent's model), /ask and /delegate --model right after the target, the web UI's Run task form (a Model list of what the chosen peer or this agent lets you pick, see MDL-10) and the model argument of the MCP and A2A delegate; the plan editor and builder read and write model=. The step's task carries it, the plan check warns when every peer a step may go to says it doesn't allow the model, the worker refuses a task asking for a model its owner doesn't allow (a refusal naming the allowed ones) and runs an allowed one, and the result, get_task and the A2A metadata name the model that did the work.

The allowlist changes what a peer may do in place (Change…: whether it may delegate, its hourly limit, its access level and its folders), keeping its name, addresses and Microsoft 365 grant: saved to peers.json and applied at once, a connected peer stays connected and learns its folders; a folder this agent doesn't share, or a peer that isn't on the allowlist, is refused. Chat only says what it means when hovered.

A task on its own can go to a squad (the web UI's Run on lists squads with an online member serving the provider, /delegate <provider>@#squad, the MCP and A2A delegate with peer #squad): its least busy member that can run it, as a plan step on the squad would, moving to another member while one turns it down or goes away before running it; its card names the member and the squad. A squad that doesn't exist, or that no member can run the task for, is refused with the reason.

A squad step or task that names a model goes to a member that allows it (as the members' hellos say; one that says nothing allows any), even when another member is less busy; if none does, it goes to the least busy as before, which refuses it saying why.

Squads are changed in place (the web UI's Change… on a squad, its name fixed; proofkin squad create replaces one), and New squad refuses a name that is taken; members that left the allowlist are listed so they can be dropped. Bad squad and member names are refused in words about squads and peers.

The squad dialog says what each peer would take as a member: whose digital worker it is and its role, the providers it runs with their default model and reasoning, and the folders it shares (marked when they have a team plan); an offline one says that shows when it connects. A peer that runs no providers and leads no team plan (an agent that only delegates), or shares no folder, takes no squad steps, as the plan check says (sign-offs need a person): the dialog and the squads card say so and why, the card warns when no online member can take its steps, and a squad whose members all take none isn't saved.

The GitHub card says where each task branch's work is, from one GraphQL query for all of a repository's branches, checked against the repository's branch as GitHub has it (fetched when the clone's last fetch is over 5 minutes old; when it can't be, the card says the states are as of the last fetch): its newest pull request (open, merged or closed, and whether it has the branch as it is), its commit or its changes (the same content in every file it changes) on the repository's branch already, the issues it is for all closed (and the pull requests from other branches that closed them, named on the card, in Review changes and in the delete confirmation as possibly having its work), and its commits, files and lines that aren't there. A branch is safe to delete only when its work is on the repository's branch or a pull request merged it as it is: closed issues, a closed pull request, or one that merged an earlier version of it don't make it safe. The card offers only Delete branch then, as nothing is left to review (on GitHub first, then in the clone, only p2p/ branches); Review changes and Delete branch, its confirmation saying what is lost, once its pull request was closed as it is or its issues are all closed (it isn't proposed again); Review changes and Open PR while there is work to merge and no pull request is open; and Review changes alone while one is open. It says how many older branches it doesn't show.

Review changes on a task branch (GET /api/repos/NAME/changes?branch=, only p2p/ branches of a linked repository) shows what a pull request from it would carry before it is opened or the branch deleted: its commits that aren't on the repository's branch (up to 50), the proof the pull request would carry, the files it changes with lines added and removed (binary files say so), and the diff from where the branches split, cut at 400 KB on a line's end and saying so; each file's lines read by its hunks' counts, shown as text (never markup). The pull request form says what it would change, with a link back to the review.

A pull request a plan's pull request step opens lists the plan's sign-offs before it: each approval step it comes after, with who approved it, their agent's key, when, and their note as code (so it mentions no one and links nothing), from the record the approver's agent signed. The folder's agent lists only approvals that verify for exactly their words and were asked for by the peer that asks for the pull request, says how many it left out, and names the evidence run that has them (proofkin runs verify).

A pull request step asks the people who signed off before it to review the pull request it opens, by GitHub account: the profile's own (its GitHub sign-in) for the owner's sign-offs, and for a peer's, the account the allowlist has for it (peers allow --github, peers github, or the web UI's allowlist dialog; kept when the peer is allowed again, empty forgets it). reviewers= names others instead (me, an allowlisted peer, or a GitHub login, each once, at most 10; none asks no one; only on pull request steps), and the plan check warns about each one whose account it doesn't know, saying how to set it. The folder's agent asks GitHub for each one separately when it opens the pull request (never again for one it opened before), doesn't ask its own account (the author), and its signed result says who was asked, and who wasn't and why.

A folder that takes pull request steps can have its owner approve each one (share pull-requests --approve, or Ask me to approve each one in the web UI; peers learn that it does): the request waits in the owner's approvals saying who asks, the title, branch and commit, the sign-offs, reviewers and issues; nothing is pushed or opened until they approve, a rejection fails the step with their reason, the pull request says they approved it with their note, and one an earlier try opened isn't asked about again. A finished run's card lists the work a pull request can be opened from (each signed commit a model's step made in a peer's folder that no other step of the run builds on, unless a pull request step of the run saw it merged) and why it can't be now; Open pull request (POST /api/runs/ID/pull-request with a title and reviewers) sends the folder's agent the ask with the run's sign-offs on that work and the reviewers resolved as reviewers= does, and the pull request says who asked for it from which evidence run.

A task in a linked repository's folder starts from the repository's latest commit: before it starts, its agent fetches the repository's branch (unless the clone fetched it in the last minute) and fast-forwards the clone, telling the requester (updated folder 'app' to its repository's latest commit abc1234 (N newer commits)). The clone is left as it is when the repository can't be reached, it has another branch checked out, its branch has commits the repository's hasn't, or the update would overwrite its local changes; the task then starts from the clone's commit and its result says which one and why.

A sign-off's approver can ask for changes instead of approving or rejecting (web UI Ask for changes, terminal /changes N WHAT, POST /api/approvals/ID with changes and a note; signed as not approved, saying so) while the sign-off allows another round (changes=N on it, 0 to 5, default 2; only sign-offs take it): the steps a model did that it waits for directly are done again, each from its own earlier commit with the note, their cards saying so, then the sign-off asks again with the new results and the note it answered. A request that doesn't offer it refuses it, and asking for changes needs a note.

A plan's step can start from an earlier evidence run's work, merged or not (base=RUN:STEP; only on steps a model does in a folder, not with apply=): the commit step STEP of run RUN made, read from the run's signed record, which must check out (signatures and the patch's signed hash), is applied in its worktree first. The plan check says when the run, the step or its work isn't there, the step fails saying so if it is gone by then, and the run's report says which run's work the step started from. A run's card offers Build on it, which starts such a plan.

A task that asks for its folder's checks gives its model (Copilot or Claude; not Codex, which takes no MCP servers) a run_check tool: the worker starts proofkin task-checks as the task's MCP server proofkin-checks, which runs one of the step's checks in the task's workspace, outside the model's sandbox as the runtime does, and answers whether it passed, with its exit code, time and the end of its output (secrets redacted), at most 10 runs a task, each up to 20 minutes. A check the step doesn't name is refused, and so is an 11th run. The runtime still runs the checks after the model, and only those runs are evidence.

A model run that stops before it finishes (it runs out of time, a Copilot run being allowed up to an hour, or its provider fails) is a failed attempt: with attempts left, the next one goes on in the same worktree, told why the last run stopped, its progress saying it goes on from where the last run stopped and the result listing the stopped attempt; when it was the last attempt, what the model changed is committed to the task's branch before the error goes back, naming the branch and commit. A step whose task failed shows its peer's error alone: only a result that says it succeeded without the record its checks or sign-off need is suspect.

With a tracker linked, Plan mode and the plan editor offer Track on GitHub beside Run plan: a new issue (with a sub-issue per step), an existing issue it works on (by number) or don't track, which reads and writes the plan's track: line (a title, #N or N, off in any case; a track: line in a step's text isn't the plan's). The line under it says what running the plan does there before it runs: the repository and the board (links that open a new tab), the account the issues are assigned to, the new issue's title when the plan names one, and that anyone can read them when the repository is public (the tracker reads its visibility; tracker status says it too), or that nothing goes to GitHub. An existing issue is looked up as its number is typed (GET /api/tracker/issues/N): its title, with a warning when it is closed (running reopens it), doesn't exist (the plan would run untracked) or can't be looked up; Run plan and Schedule… ask for the number when it is missing instead of opening a new issue.

The Health card's summary counts evidence runs as passed, failed and without claims (a run without claims proves nothing, so it neither passed nor failed), leaves out counts that are zero, and shows times as durations.

A task works at a reasoning effort (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh or max): the one it asks for (a plan step's effort=, given once and not on sign-offs, team steps or @workiq steps; /ask and /delegate --effort with --model in either order; the web UI's Reasoning field; the MCP and A2A delegate's effort), else the profile's default for the provider (proofkin models effort, or models default --effort), which peers learn from the hello (a hello without one reads as none). The worker refuses a name that isn't an effort, and one its owner doesn't allow (MDL-7). Copilot gets it fitted to what the task's model supports (the nearest it supports below the one asked for, none if it supports none, and the task runs at the model's own if the CLI refuses it); Claude gets low to max (minimal is low) and Codex all of them, through the bridge. The result names the model with its effort, e.g. claude-opus-5.5 (max reasoning), in characters every version of Proofkin shows as they are, and so do the signed output, the audit log and the CLI; models list shows the efforts each Copilot model supports.

Wherever a model is chosen, the default model and reasoning effort are the selected choice, named when the agent that runs the task says them: the Run task form's Model list (the default, then what the chosen peer or this agent lets you pick, see MDL-10; with Any peer or a squad, each peer's default) and Reasoning list (the default effort as the chosen model takes it, then the levels it allows that the model supports), and the plan builder's Model and Reasoning fields for the step's peer. The This agent card lists the model and effort each provider's tasks run at, and the models and efforts peers may ask for; a boss that only delegates lists what its digital workers run.

A digital worker runs on its owner's model settings (default model, allowed models, reasoning effort and allowed efforts) for each provider it sets nothing for, as it runs on its owner's accounts: its agent, its executor, its hello and the web UI use them, and a running worker follows them when they change (MDL-8), and proofkin models list says which are its owner's; a provider it sets anything for runs on its own setting.

A step that names an issue (issue=#N) on a tracked run gets the issue's title and body, as its tracker has them, in front of its task as external content (Proofkin's own markers left out, secrets redacted, cut at 20,000 characters saying how much was left out and where the whole issue is; after the earlier steps' results), so the plan needn't repeat them and the model needn't look them up; a sign-off shows them to the person. Its commit is titled with the issue's title, the step's own first line under it. Steps that name no issue get none.

Putting issues on the board (Add existing issues, tracker add, and a tracked run's issues) holds when GitHub answers a batch of adds with an error: each add that fails is looked up on the board first, as GitHub may have carried it out (an HTTP 502 for a batch it did) or put it there itself (a board's Auto-add sub-issues workflow adds a run's sub-issues when the run's issue goes on it, and adding them then says "Content already exists in this project"); those still missing are added again, five to a request, and only what still fails is a problem, once. Every item it added gets its status (and a run's items their agent). Queries GitHub answers with a 502, 503 or 504 are asked again, twice at most; mutations never are.

A profile's owner chooses the reasoning efforts tasks may ask a provider for (proofkin models allow <provider> --efforts <levels>|any, with or without models; the web UI's Models dialog), kept least to most in profile.json (all six is any, and left out). The default effort must be one of them, and the list keep it. A task asking for another is refused before it runs, naming the allowed ones; one asking for none works at the default, else the least allowed. Peers learn the list from the hello (a hello without one reads as any), cleaned of names that aren't efforts; a squad step with effort= goes first to members that allow it, and the plan check warns when every peer the step may go to says it doesn't.

claims.claim: A worker lists the models its Copilot account offers once it runs and tells peers the usable ones its tasks may ask for (only the allowed ones when it limits them), each with its name, vendor, cost multiplier and the reasoning efforts it supports (known efforts only, least to most), in its hello and, whenever its settings or that list change, in a models message older peers ignore; peers keep only well-formed, usable offers, at most 200 per provider, for the providers it serves. A running agent applies a change to its profile.json, and a digital worker to its owner's for the providers it sets nothing for, within seconds and without a restart: its next tasks run with them and its connected peers learn them.

claims.claim: The web UI's Models dialog (Models… on the This agent card, and on each digital worker) lists the models the account offers, by vendor, to allow any or only those ticked (named for a provider that lists none), the reasoning levels to allow, and the defaults. Saving checks the settings as a whole (the defaults must be allowed; a provider the agent doesn't run, or an agent that isn't one of its digital workers, is refused and nothing is saved), writes profile.json and applies them at once: this agent's tasks and peers use them, and a digital worker uses its own or, again, its owner's. An agent that only delegates lists the models for its digital workers with a Copilot CLI started for the purpose.

The Run task form and the plan builder list what the chosen peer lets you pick: the models it allows, else all its account offers (by vendor, with their cost multiplier; a name typed by hand only for a peer that lists none), and the reasoning levels it allows that the chosen model supports, its defaults selected (the default level as the model takes it; a model without levels says so), the levels changing with the model. For Any peer or a squad they list what their peers allow together, and an Any peer task that names a model or an effort goes to a peer that allows them.

An agent blueprint (proofkin.agent-blueprint/v1) is checked against the profile it is for: its skills, knowledge topics, folders with their checks and MCP servers, the providers it is signed in to, the models and efforts it allows, approvers on its allowlist and unique requirement ids, and a name nothing else has. Each problem has a stable code, is an error or a warning, and says what is wrong, how to fix it and the JSON pointer of the field. Asking for more than it needs (full access with no check, every tool of a server, every Work IQ source, delegation, instructions that ask for tools) is a least-privilege warning naming the narrower choice (AC-6).

A task records the usage its provider reported: the Copilot session's tokens and premium requests, the Claude Agent SDK's tokens and cost estimate, and the tokens of Codex's turn. A provider that reports none records none, not zero. Usage adds up over a task's attempts, goes back to the requester with the result (older peers ignore it) and is kept in the worker's audit entry, which holds no prompt or output text. The web UI shows it on a finished task and in the audit, and proofkin audit sums it per peer and provider.

claims.claim: The profile's factory keeps drafts, and each agent's lifecycle state and history (who, when, what), in its factory folder: written atomically under a lock, for its owner only. They survive restarts and concurrent writers, a damaged file is reported with its path and left as it is, a name has one agent, and an agent with releases is never deleted. proofkin factory list, show, edit, check and delete work on them: edit takes the blueprint from an editor, a file or stdin and keeps it with its problems (text that isn't JSON or renames the agent isn't saved), and check fails while a draft has errors, showing each with its fix.

An agent's eval suite has cases that each name the requirement they prove, give a task, its fixtures and what to expect, and every requirement needs a case with a deterministic expectation (AC-10). contains, not-contains, regex, json-schema, max-words, files-changed and check expectations pass and fail as the design says (check runs the folder's check in the run's folder); a judge rubric is scored by a model, never graded here. Fixtures must be files in the agent's fixtures folder, reached without links.

proofkin factory templates lists the built-in templates with their purpose, most access and number of eval cases. Each passes validation unchanged with a case for every requirement, and proofkin factory new --template makes a draft from one with no model, on the providers the profile is signed in to (AC-4).

proofkin factory new --describe has the profile's default model write a draft from the owner's words: read-only, in an empty folder, given what the profile has as data and the description with secrets redacted. The draft is checked, and its problems go back to the model, at most 3 tries in all; then the owner gets the last draft with its problems (AC-1, AC-2). Its provenance records the provider, model, effort, template, the SHA-256 of the description (not its text), the time and the tries. Drafting grants nothing, whatever the description says (AC-3, TM-1), and needs a provider the profile is signed in to.

claims.claim: proofkin factory build turns a draft without errors into the files an agent is made of: its agent file (front matter with its name, purpose, skills and MCP servers, never tools or a model; then its instructions, the requirements its answers must meet and the rules every factory agent follows, a request outside its purpose answered with one OUT_OF_SCOPE line), its blueprint, its eval suite, the skills it follows under its own names and its team plan, which must be a valid team plan and needs delegation. The same blueprint builds the same bytes on every platform (keys sorted, LF line endings), and changing any field changes the build's hash, the SHA-256 of its files' sha256sum listing. A build is kept once by its hash, written whole, and checked against its hash whenever it is read: one changed after it was built is refused. proofkin factory show lists an agent's builds.

claims.claim: What a blueprint asks for is resolved against what its owner offers in each folder it is deployed to (proofkin factory check, its deploy folders or --folders): its tasks get at most the folder's access, the MCP servers it offers to tasks with that access, with the tools asked for, and the checks it has. What isn't offered is an error naming the command that offers it (share add keeping the folder's checks and worktrees, mcp add, mcp resume, plugin enable), and a server that offers fewer tools than every tool asked for is a warning. Resolving never shares a folder, offers a server or grants a peer anything: the shares and the allowlist are byte-identical after it (AC-5). What one blueprint asks for beyond another (more access, servers or tools, checks, Microsoft 365 sources, delegation, a new or changed team plan) is listed, for a release's sign-off.

An agent is evaluated on its blueprint's candidate models, else on its providers' defaults in the profile's model settings. A candidate is left out, with the reason, when the profile isn't signed in to its provider or doesn't allow its model or effort, the account doesn't offer it or its policy disables it, it is over max_multiplier or has no multiplier, it can't use the MCP servers the agent needs (Codex), or the agent's Microsoft 365 content would go outside the owner's own workers; proofkin factory show lists both. Among the candidates an evaluation passed, the recommendation follows the blueprint's prefer (cost, latency or quality; what isn't known counts as worst, and ties go to the first listed), and pinning it gives the model settings that keep a deployment's tasks to the models that passed.

A digital worker's memory (proofkin worker memory) puts its context topics, copied with their Microsoft 365 marks from its owner's knowledge, in front of every task it serves, as external content, at most 24,000 characters; a marked topic only for a requester who may have its labels (its owner, known by its endpoint id, or a peer whose grant names them). The task's signed output records that knowledge by hash, and its evidence the labels of marked knowledge, never its text; the requester marks what it does with the result with them: a later step goes only to a peer granted them (one done again for a sign-off too), what it saves is marked, a mark without labels still counts as unlabeled, and a lead's team results go back only to a requester who may have what any of its steps held (their evidence, failed steps included, and the lead's own Microsoft 365 content), their labels in its evidence (AC-30). Each task names the labels of what it holds, which its worker's evidence repeats. A task whose checks passed adds a lesson to the worker's lessons topic, once, capped, marked with the labels of what the task was given (unknown if its model read Work IQ itself); one whose checks failed adds none, and lessons older than the retention are removed (AC-31).
